name: Kathakali
tagline: Kerala’s classical dance‑drama of painted faces and epic stories
summary: Kathakali is Kerala’s classical dance‑drama—stylised gestures, elaborate makeup (chutti) and towering costumes that act out episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and other tales.
description: Kathakali is a classical dance‑drama from Kerala that combines music, stylised acting, hand gestures (mudras), facial expression and long, ritualised make‑up and costuming to narrate stories from Hindu epics and Puranic literature.

The fully developed form emerges around the 17th century from earlier ritual and palace theatre traditions (Ramanattam, Krishnanattam and local temple arts). Its visual language—pachcha, kathi, thadi, kari and minukku makeup types and the white chutti frame—signals character types before a word is sung.

Visitors see Kathakali in two main settings: traditional, often night‑long temple or festival productions and shortened demonstration shows designed for travellers (make‑up demo + excerpted performance). Training and scholarly preservation continue at institutions such as Kerala Kalamandalam and Margi.
A live Kathakali experience gives you close access to the slow, codified acting (the 'eyes' work), percussion and vocal music that together make Kathakali both a theatre and a devotional art.
highlights: Elaborate face makeup (pachcha, kathi, thadi, kari, minukku) and the white chutti frame
Highly codified gestures (mudras) and nine rasas expressed by eye and face work
Full‑length, overnight plays at temples and condensed evening shows for visitors
Major training centres: Kerala Kalamandalam (Cheruthuruthy) and Margi (Thiruvananthapuram)
Repertoire drawn from Ramayana, Mahabharata and classical literature

sections.heading: Background
body: Kathakali literally means 'story-play' (katha = story, kali = play). It grows from temple and court performance traditions in Kerala and reaches its classical form by the 17th century, influenced by earlier forms such as Krishnanattam and Ramanattam.

Makeup and costume are a built, symbolic language: green (pachcha) for noble/ divine heroes, kathi (knife) for arrogant villains, thadi (bearded) for certain anti‑heroes and demonic types, kari (black) and minukku (luminous) for other categories. The white chutti rim and tall headgear complete the transformation.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend a museum or cultural‑centre evening show in Kochi, Munnar or Thekkady to watch the make‑up ritual and a condensed excerpt (these usually run under 90 minutes and focus on demonstration and a single episode). For a fuller experience, seek a temple festival or a production by Kerala Kalamandalam or Margi, which stage longer, dramaturgically complete plays.

Watch the makeup room (chutti application and face painting) — many visitor shows open the makeup area so you can see artists prepare for up to two hours before performance. Also notice the live percussion (chenda, maddalam, idakka) and the vocalists who narrate the story.

If you want hands‑on experience, short workshops and short‑term courses are available at Kerala Kalamandalam and other training centres; these institutions also host public performances and lecture‑demonstrations.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Major hubs: Kochi (Fort Kochi cultural venues and Kerala Kathakali Centre), Cheruthuruthy (Kerala Kalamandalam, Thrissur district) and Thiruvananthapuram (Margi). Fly to Cochin (COK) or Thiruvananthapuram (TRV) then travel by road/rail to your chosen centre.

Confirm schedules ahead: tourist demonstration shows run most evenings at cultural centres, but full‑length traditional performances depend on temple festivals and institutional calendars. Expect the makeup process to begin an hour or more before the staged excerpt.

latest.text: Kerala Kalamandalam holds its 96th Annual Celebration (events and performances at the Kalamandalam Koothambalam in Cheruthuruthy, Nov 7–9, 2026).

The Ministry of Culture–supported 17th Kathakali Festival (Kalakshetra Foundation, Chennai) brings Kerala Kalamandalam, Margi and Sadanam together for three days of productions and lecture‑demonstrations (18–20 Sep 2026).

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (post‑monsoon and festival season for the clearest weather and many performances).
visitorInfo.howToReach: Fly to Kochi (Cochin International) or Thiruvananthapuram, then travel by road or rail to Kochi cultural centres, Cheruthuruthy (Kalamandalam, Thrissur district) or Margi (Thiruvananthapuram). Local cultural centres in tourist towns run regular evening make‑up demonstrations.
etiquette: Arrive early — the make‑up room is often the most revealing part of the experience.
Ask about photography rules: some venues allow photos of the makeup but restrict flash or stage photography during performance.
For a full traditional experience, check temple festival calendars or book performances by established schools (Kalamandalam, Margi); short tourist shows are a good introduction but are condensed.
Confirm show dates and start times with the venue before you travel.
